text: Was the disappearance of all your courses related to the course-selection computer system (e.g., a system crash, error, or being timed out of the enrollment session)?
Did the loss of your courses result from an action taken by another person (e.g., someone else accessing your account and dropping/altering them)?
Did the other person drop or remove your courses intentionally, knowing it would affect you (rather than through a mistake or accident)?
Did the other person take your courses because they wanted those course spots/timeslots for themselves (i.e., competition for enrollment places), rather than as a prank, revenge, or other motive?
Was the other person someone you know personally (e.g., a friend, classmate, roommate, or family member)?
Did the other person use your account credentials without your permission to remove the courses?
Did the other person act through an official/administrative channel (e.g., an instructor, department, or university staff removing you from courses), rather than accessing your account directly?
Did the other person use your own logged-in device or session (e.g., you left your computer/phone logged in and they used it) to drop the courses?
Were your courses all gone because another person enrolled in them and thereby occupied/bumped you from those courses (rather than deleting your existing enrollment)?
Did the other person remove your courses by exploiting a flaw or loophole in the enrollment system (e.g., hacking or abusing a bug), rather than through normal use of the system?

Did the other person remove your courses through normal use of the enrollment system without needing your account or a system flaw (for example, by a legitimate administrative-sounding action available to ordinary users, like forcing a swap/drop through a shared function)?
Did the other person remove your courses only after the two of you had some interaction or agreement (e.g., you asked them to help or gave them some form of access/consent)?
Did you give this person something of value (e.g., money or a favor) in exchange for their taking or manipulating your course enrollment?
Did you ask this person to help you with course enrollment (e.g., to help you get into or secure courses), and that help somehow resulted in your courses being removed?
Did you let this person use your account or enrollment credentials voluntarily (e.g., you shared your password or let them log in), and they later dropped the courses?
Did the interaction between you and this person involve a promise or deal in which you would get the courses you wanted, but it turned out to be a scam/trap that left you with no courses?

Was the interaction a request where you asked the person to enroll you in courses on your behalf (e.g., you gave them your course list/selection and asked them to add you), and they instead did something that removed your enrollment?

Was the interaction unrelated to the enrollment system itself — for example, you had a personal conversation or conflict with the person beforehand, and their removal of your courses was a consequence of that?
Did this person remove your courses as an act of revenge or retaliation for something you did to them (rather than punishment for a rule violation)?

Did the person remove your courses for a reason connected to your academic conduct or a rule violation (e.g., you were caught violating an academic rule, and their action was a form of discipline/report)?
Was the personal interaction romantic in nature (e.g., you rejected the person, or a relationship ended), and their removal of your courses was motivated by that?

Did you and this person have a conflict or quarrel over a shared matter such as a group project, roommate situation, or competition (not romantic), and the removal of your courses was a consequence of that conflict?
Did you cause harm or offense to this person unintentionally (e.g., an accident, a misunderstanding, or a careless act), and they removed your courses in reaction to that?
Did you intentionally do something that harmed or offended this person (e.g., an insult, betrayal, or deliberate slight), prompting them to remove your courses?
Did you ask this person a favor or for help with something (e.g., borrowing something, advice, or assistance), and after that interaction they had the ability/opportunity to remove your courses?
Did the favor/help involve lending the person your University account or student card (or other physical credential) rather than a purely verbal interaction?
Did you ask this person to help you with something academic (e.g., homework, an assignment, studying, or tutoring)?
Did the favor involve borrowing money from or lending money to this person?
Did you ask this person to use their enrollment account or their status as a student (e.g., to help you add a course, or use their course quota), rather than borrowing a physical item?
Did the favor involve borrowing a physical item from this person (e.g., a book, notes, or an object)?
Did you ask this person for help that required them to be present at or act on a computer/device (e.g., help with an online task), giving them access to your courses?
Did you ask this person to keep a secret or help you conceal something (e.g., cover for you), and when the situation went wrong they retaliated by dropping your courses?
Was the favor you asked of this person related to course enrollment at all (even indirectly, e.g., asking them about courses, which courses to take, or when to enroll)?

Did you ask this person for something that was within the university (e.g., a campus-related favor like using their room, printer, or facilities), rather than something personal/social outside school?
Did you ask this person to keep something for you or hold onto something for you (e.g., to hand something in or deliver something on your behalf)?
Did you ask this person about scheduling/logistics for something other than courses (e.g., a meeting time or event), and does the answer hinge on miscommunication about a deadline?
Was the favor related to food (e.g., asking them to buy or bring you food)?
Did this food-related interaction happen on the same evening when all your courses were gone (e.g., you were away getting or eating food, or the person was acting while handling your food)?
Did you ask this person to use a food delivery app or online service (e.g., order food or use their account) on a shared platform, rather than simply buying/bringing you food?
Did you ask this person to order or buy food for you on a delivery platform where your account/course-related information was accessible, so that the removal happened during that transaction?
Did you ask this person for food in a way that involved your phone or device being handed to them (e.g., they used your phone to order food)?
Did you ask this person to bring you food because you were busy or occupied (e.g., you were at your computer doing course enrollment/selection)?
Was the person who removed your courses a food delivery courier or restaurant worker you interacted with over an order, rather than a fellow student you know?

Did the courier/restaurant worker obtain access to your enrollment account through details you gave them while ordering food (e.g., you shared your phone/computer or login information as part of the food transaction)?

Did the food interaction involve you giving the courier/worker your student card, phone, or other item as a pledge/payment (e.g., for a delivery you couldn't pay for), which they then used to access your enrollment?
Did the food interaction involve a payment issue (e.g., card declined, wrong order, or you couldn't pay) that led to the courier/worker doing something to your account?

Did the courier/restaurant worker access the university system via a public or shared computer (e.g., a computer you used in a common area or the courier's own route/terminal) where you were still logged in?
Was the courier/worker motivated by something beyond just the food delivery—for example, they had a personal grudge against you or targeted you specifically regardless of food?

Did the courier/worker remove your courses using the course-selection system's legitimate interface (rather than hacking or a bug) after somehow obtaining your account access during the food transaction?

Did the courier/worker remove your courses indirectly, without ever touching a computer or your account themselves (e.g., by telling you something false that made you act, or by interfering in a system by non-digital means)?
Was the removal of your courses done by the courier/worker deliberately and directly through a digital action of their own?
Is the food interaction a red herring or minor detail, with the real mechanism being something else entirely (e.g., your courses were dropped by an automated process or by yourself unknowingly)?
Did you ask this courier/worker for something as a favor beyond a normal food delivery (e.g., to buy something for you, run an errand, or help with something so they came into your room/residence)?
Did the courier/worker come to your room or residence hall as part of the delivery, and did that give them access to your logged-in computer or your student account information?
Did the courier/worker tamper with your food (e.g., spit in it, adulterate it) as part of the incident?
Did you ask the courier/worker to bring the food to a particular place (e.g., a computer lab or library) where the course-selection system was being used on a shared/public computer?
Was the food delivery made to your home or dorm, and did the worker gain entry to your residence (e.g., you let them in, or they came inside)?
Did the removal of your courses occur because the courier/worker took your food back or you refused the delivery, i.e., was the incident fundamentally a dispute about the order itself?

Did you leave your logged-in computer or phone unattended in a public/common area (e.g., library, canteen, or lobby) while you dealt with the food delivery, allowing the worker to access it without entering your residence?
Did the food-related interaction involve you calling or texting the courier (e.g., to give directions or delivery instructions) using your phone, rather than meeting in person?
